name: Transformer
coreMechanism: Self-attention and feed-forward layers arranged in a stacked neural architecture.
attention: Multi-head self-attention
positionEncoding: Original formulation uses sinusoidal positional encoding.
routing: Dense computation.
sequenceModeling: Attention-based sequence modeling with direct pairwise interaction between token representations.
strengths: Foundation for modern language, vision, speech, and multimodal architectures
limitations: Self-attention has quadratic sequence-length complexity in the original formulation
Memory requirements increase substantially with sequence length

name: Encoder-Only Transformer
coreMechanism: Bidirectional Transformer encoder that builds contextual representations from both directions of the input sequence.
attention: Bidirectional self-attention
routing: Dense computation.
sequenceModeling: Bidirectional contextual representation learning.
strengths: Effective for classification and token-level prediction
limitations: Not naturally optimized for autoregressive text generation
Full attention can become expensive for long sequences

name: Decoder-Only Transformer
coreMechanism: Autoregressive Transformer architecture that predicts subsequent tokens using causal self-attention.
attention: Causal self-attention
positionEncoding: Model-dependent; may use learned positional embeddings, RoPE, ALiBi, or other mechanisms.
feedForward: Position-wise feed-forward network or gated feed-forward variant.
normalization: Layer normalization or RMSNorm depending on model family.
routing: Dense or sparse depending on the model.
sequenceModeling: Autoregressive next-token prediction.
strengths: Natural fit for generative language modeling
Supports general-purpose generation and tool-oriented applications
limitations: Autoregressive generation is sequential at inference time
Long-context attention can be computationally expensive

name: Encoder-Decoder Transformer
coreMechanism: Separate encoder and decoder stacks connected through cross-attention.
attention: Encoder self-attention, decoder causal self-attention, and encoder-decoder cross-attention.
routing: Dense computation in the original formulation.
sequenceModeling: Sequence-to-sequence transformation.
strengths: Effective for translation and text-to-text tasks
Explicit separation between input encoding and output generation
limitations: More computational components than a single-stack architecture
Cross-attention introduces additional computation

name: Masked Language Modeling
coreMechanism: Training objective in which portions of the input sequence are masked and the model learns to reconstruct the missing information.
attention: Typically bidirectional self-attention when implemented with an encoder architecture.
routing: Usually dense, but architecture-dependent.
sequenceModeling: Bidirectional contextual prediction over corrupted input.
strengths: Supports token-level and sentence-level downstream tasks
limitations: Not itself a complete architectural specification
Masking creates a pretraining distribution that differs from ordinary generation

name: Causal Language Model
coreMechanism: Autoregressive prediction of the next token conditioned on preceding tokens.
attention: Causal self-attention in Transformer implementations.
routing: Dense or sparse depending on architecture.
sequenceModeling: Left-to-right autoregressive sequence modeling.
strengths: Scales effectively with model and data size
Supports text generation and in-context learning
limitations: Generation is sequential
Long sequences can create substantial attention and memory costs

name: Mixture-of-Experts Transformer
coreMechanism: Routes each input token through a subset of specialized feed-forward experts using a learned routing mechanism.
attention: Typically self-attention combined with sparse expert layers.
feedForward: Multiple expert feed-forward networks with sparse activation.
routing: Learned sparse token-to-expert routing.
sequenceModeling: Transformer-based sequence modeling with conditional computation.
strengths: Lower active computation than dense models of comparable total size
limitations: Routing can create load imbalance
Expert communication can increase distributed-system complexity
Training stability can be sensitive to routing design

name: Sparse Mixture of Experts
coreMechanism: A collection of expert subnetworks in which a router activates only a small number of experts for each input.
attention: Architecture-dependent.
routing: Sparse learned routing, commonly top-k expert selection.
sequenceModeling: Conditional computation over token representations.
limitations: Expert routing introduces communication overhead
Load balancing is a major systems and optimization concern
Total parameter count can greatly exceed active parameter count

name: State Space Model
coreMechanism: Models sequence dynamics through latent state transitions rather than relying exclusively on pairwise attention.
attention: No conventional full self-attention is required by the core state-space formulation.
positionEncoding: Sequence order is represented through state evolution.
routing: Dense sequential state update.
sequenceModeling: Latent-state sequence propagation.
strengths: Linear-time sequence processing in many formulations
limitations: Training and optimization can be more specialized than standard Transformers
Architectural behavior differs substantially from attention-based models

name: Selective State Space Model
coreMechanism: State-space sequence model whose parameters are selectively dependent on the input, allowing the model to control which information is retained or forgotten.
attention: Does not require conventional full self-attention.
positionEncoding: Sequence order is encoded through recurrent state evolution.
routing: Input-dependent selective state updates.
sequenceModeling: Input-conditioned recurrent state-space processing.
limitations: Different computational characteristics from Transformer attention
Less mature ecosystem than standard Transformer architectures

name: Hybrid Transformer–State Space Architecture
coreMechanism: Combines Transformer attention layers with state-space or recurrent sequence-processing layers.
attention: Selective Transformer attention combined with state-space sequence blocks.
routing: Architecture-dependent.
sequenceModeling: Hybrid attention and state-space sequence processing.
strengths: Combines attention-based retrieval with efficient sequence processing
limitations: More complex architecture
Requires careful balancing of heterogeneous sequence mechanisms

name: Recurrent Sequence Model
coreMechanism: Maintains a recurrent hidden state that is updated as sequence elements are processed.
attention: Optional; not required by the core architecture.
positionEncoding: Implicitly represented through recurrent state transitions.
routing: Sequential recurrent state update.
sequenceModeling: Explicit recurrent state propagation.
strengths: Can operate with constant-size recurrent memory
limitations: Sequential computation can reduce training parallelism
Long-range dependency learning can be difficult in classical recurrent architectures

name: Diffusion Model
coreMechanism: Learns to generate data by reversing a progressive noising process.
attention: Optional and architecture-dependent.
routing: Usually dense computation.
sequenceModeling: Not fundamentally sequence-based; generation proceeds through iterative denoising steps.
limitations: Generation can require many iterative denoising steps
Sampling can be computationally expensive
Training and inference involve specialized objectives

name: Latent Diffusion
coreMechanism: Performs diffusion in a compressed latent representation rather than directly in pixel space.
attention: Often uses cross-attention for conditioning.
feedForward: Typically implemented through a U-Net or related denoising architecture.
routing: Usually dense computation.
sequenceModeling: Iterative denoising in latent space.
strengths: Lower computational cost than full pixel-space diffusion
limitations: Quality depends on the learned latent autoencoder
Still requires iterative sampling

name: Diffusion Transformer
coreMechanism: Uses Transformer blocks as the denoising network inside a diffusion generation process.
attention: Transformer self-attention.
routing: Dense or sparse depending on implementation.
sequenceModeling: Transformer-based representation processing during iterative denoising.
strengths: Scales Transformer representation learning to diffusion
Strong modeling capacity for high-dimensional generation
limitations: Attention can be computationally expensive at high spatial resolutions
Sampling remains iterative

name: U-Net
coreMechanism: Encoder-decoder convolutional architecture with skip connections between corresponding resolution levels.
attention: Optional; modern variants may include attention blocks.
positionEncoding: Spatial structure is represented through convolutional feature maps.
routing: Dense convolutional computation.
sequenceModeling: Spatial feature processing rather than token sequence modeling.
limitations: Computational cost increases with spatial resolution
Less naturally scalable to generic sequence modeling than Transformers

name: Convolutional Neural Network
coreMechanism: Uses local convolutional filters to build hierarchical spatial representations.
attention: Not required by the core architecture.
positionEncoding: Spatial locality is encoded through convolutional receptive fields.
routing: Dense local spatial computation.
sequenceModeling: Spatial rather than sequential modeling.
strengths: Strong inductive bias for spatial data
limitations: Global interactions require deeper layers or additional mechanisms
Less flexible than attention for some large-scale multimodal architectures

name: Residual Network
coreMechanism: Adds shortcut connections around layers so networks can learn residual transformations.
attention: Not required by the core architecture.
positionEncoding: Spatial information is encoded through convolution.
normalization: Typically batch normalization in classical variants.
routing: Dense computation.
sequenceModeling: Hierarchical spatial feature extraction.
limitations: Primarily designed for spatial representation learning
Global relationships are less direct than in attention architectures

name: Vision Transformer
coreMechanism: Represents an image as a sequence of patches and processes those patches using Transformer blocks.
attention: Multi-head self-attention over image patches.
positionEncoding: Positional embeddings or architecture-specific positional representations.
routing: Dense or sparse depending on variant.
sequenceModeling: Patch-token sequence modeling.
strengths: Can integrate naturally with multimodal language models
limitations: Attention cost grows with the number of visual tokens
May require substantial data or pretraining for strong performance

name: Multimodal Encoder
coreMechanism: Encodes information from multiple modalities into compatible or shared representations.
attention: Often uses Transformer attention within or across modalities.
routing: Dense or modality-specific computation.
sequenceModeling: Joint representation learning across modality-specific token sequences.
strengths: Provides a foundation for multimodal generation and understanding
limitations: Alignment between modalities can be difficult
Different modalities have substantially different statistical structures

name: Cross-Attention Architecture
coreMechanism: Allows one representation sequence to attend to another representation sequence.
attention: Query representations attend to keys and values from another sequence.
positionEncoding: Inherited from the connected modality or sequence architecture.
routing: Attention-based information routing between representations.
sequenceModeling: Conditional interaction between separate sequences or modalities.
limitations: Additional computational cost
Alignment quality depends on learned representations

name: Multimodal Fusion
coreMechanism: Combines representations from different modalities into a shared or conditionally interacting representation space.
attention: Often implemented with cross-attention or joint self-attention.
routing: Cross-modal or joint representation routing.
sequenceModeling: Joint processing of modality-specific token sequences.
strengths: Allows interaction between text, image, audio, video, or other modalities
limitations: Requires careful modality alignment
Multimodal tokenization can significantly increase computational cost

name: Dual Encoder
coreMechanism: Uses separate encoders for two input modalities or input types and maps them into a shared embedding space.
attention: Architecture-dependent within each encoder.
routing: Independent encoding followed by representation comparison.
sequenceModeling: Separate sequence encoding into fixed-dimensional representations.
limitations: Independent encoding limits direct token-level interaction
Fine-grained cross-input reasoning can be weaker than cross-attention

name: Cross Encoder
coreMechanism: Jointly encodes two inputs so their tokens can directly interact through shared attention.
attention: Joint self-attention over combined input representations.
feedForward: Transformer feed-forward layers or architecture-specific equivalents.
routing: Joint attention-based interaction.
sequenceModeling: Joint sequence encoding for pairwise comparison.
strengths: Effective for reranking and relevance estimation
limitations: More expensive than dual-encoder retrieval
Inputs generally need to be processed together

name: Embedding Model
coreMechanism: Maps inputs into continuous vector representations designed to capture semantic or task-relevant relationships.
attention: Architecture-dependent.
routing: Architecture-dependent.
sequenceModeling: Encodes sequences or other inputs into fixed-dimensional representations.
limitations: A single vector can compress information
Embedding quality depends strongly on training objective and domain

name: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
coreMechanism: Retrieves external documents or knowledge items and conditions a generative model on the retrieved information.
attention: Typically uses Transformer attention within the generator and may use cross-attention or concatenation for retrieved context.
routing: Retriever selects relevant external information before or during generation.
sequenceModeling: Combines retrieved context with autoregressive or sequence-to-sequence generation.
strengths: Provides access to external or updated knowledge
Allows domain-specific knowledge without retraining the entire generator
limitations: Retrieval errors propagate into generation
Context-window limitations constrain the amount of retrieved information
Requires additional retrieval infrastructure
Generated answers can still contradict retrieved evidence

name: Retriever–Generator Architecture
coreMechanism: Separates information retrieval from generative modeling, allowing a retriever to select evidence that conditions a generator.
attention: Generator attention is architecture-dependent; retrieved representations may be incorporated through cross-attention or concatenation.
positionEncoding: Inherited from the generator and retriever.
routing: Retriever determines which external representations reach the generator.
sequenceModeling: Retrieved evidence is integrated into downstream sequence generation.
strengths: Explicit separation between retrieval and generation
Can reduce dependence on parametric memory
limitations: Retriever quality strongly affects generation
Requires indexing and retrieval infrastructure
Joint optimization can be difficult

name: Efficient Attention Architecture
coreMechanism: Modifies full self-attention to reduce computational or memory requirements for long sequences.
attention: Sparse, linear, low-rank, local, grouped, or otherwise optimized attention.
routing: Attention pattern determines which sequence elements interact.
sequenceModeling: Long-sequence modeling with reduced attention complexity.
limitations: Approximation or sparsity can reduce access to global interactions
Different efficient-attention methods involve different accuracy and systems trade-offs

name: Sparse Attention
coreMechanism: Restricts attention connections so each token attends only to selected positions rather than the complete sequence.
attention: Structured sparse attention.
routing: Predefined or learned sparse attention pattern.
sequenceModeling: Selective long-range and local token interaction.
strengths: Can preserve important local and global interactions through structured patterns
limitations: Attention pattern design affects quality
May miss interactions excluded by the sparse pattern

name: Linear Attention
coreMechanism: Reformulates attention computation to reduce the dependence of computational cost on sequence length.
attention: Kernelized, factorized, recurrent, or otherwise linearized attention.
routing: Linearized interaction between queries and key-value representations.
sequenceModeling: Efficient long-sequence processing.
strengths: Potentially linear complexity with sequence length
Suitable for long-context and streaming applications
limitations: Linearization can change the behavior of standard softmax attention
Quality depends strongly on the chosen formulation

name: Long-Context Transformer
coreMechanism: Transformer architecture optimized through attention, positional, memory, or inference techniques for substantially longer sequences.
attention: Full, sparse, sliding-window, grouped, or other efficient attention mechanisms.
positionEncoding: May use extended positional representations or relative-position methods.
routing: Attention and memory mechanisms determine information access.
sequenceModeling: Long-range sequence modeling.
strengths: Handles large documents and extended conversations
Useful for document analysis and long-form reasoning
limitations: Longer context does not guarantee effective use of every token
Memory and compute requirements remain substantial for many implementations

name: Byte-Level Language Model
coreMechanism: Processes raw bytes or byte-derived representations rather than relying exclusively on conventional subword tokenization.
attention: Architecture-dependent.
routing: Architecture-dependent.
sequenceModeling: Sequence modeling over byte-level representations.
strengths: Avoids dependence on a fixed subword vocabulary
Naturally handles arbitrary text and symbols
limitations: Byte sequences are longer than subword token sequences
Longer input sequences can increase computational requirements

name: Token-Free Language Model
coreMechanism: Processes text without conventional subword tokenization by operating directly on characters, bytes, patches, or other lower-level representations.
attention: Architecture-dependent.
routing: Architecture-dependent.
sequenceModeling: Sequence modeling over non-subword representations.
strengths: Handles unusual strings and multilingual text naturally
Reduces sensitivity to tokenizer vocabulary boundaries
limitations: Raw representations can produce much longer sequences
Efficient processing becomes an important architectural challenge

name: Audio Transformer
coreMechanism: Represents audio or acoustic features as sequences and processes them using Transformer attention.
attention: Self-attention over acoustic or audio tokens.
routing: Attention-based temporal interaction.
sequenceModeling: Temporal acoustic sequence modeling.
strengths: Integrates naturally with multimodal Transformer systems
limitations: Audio produces high-density sequences
Attention cost can become substantial for long recordings

name: Speech Encoder-Decoder
coreMechanism: Encodes acoustic signals and transforms their representations into textual or other sequential outputs.
attention: Encoder self-attention, decoder self-attention, and optional cross-attention.
routing: Encoder representations are routed to the output decoder.
sequenceModeling: Speech-to-text or speech-to-sequence transformation.
strengths: Direct mapping between acoustic and linguistic representations
Can combine acoustic and language modeling
limitations: Audio input is computationally dense
Performance depends on robust acoustic representation learning

name: Audio Self-Supervised Encoder
coreMechanism: Learns speech representations from unlabeled audio through self-supervised prediction or contrastive objectives.
attention: Typically Transformer-based contextual encoding.
routing: Temporal contextualization through self-attention.
sequenceModeling: Contextual acoustic representation learning.
strengths: Transfers to recognition and classification tasks
limitations: Pretraining can require large-scale audio
Raw audio representation learning can be computationally expensive

name: Video Transformer
coreMechanism: Represents video as spatial-temporal tokens and applies Transformer-based attention across frames and spatial regions.
attention: Spatial, temporal, or joint spatiotemporal attention.
routing: Attention routes information across space and time.
sequenceModeling: Spatiotemporal sequence modeling.
strengths: Supports video understanding and generation systems
limitations: Video produces very large token counts
Spatiotemporal attention can be computationally expensive

name: Vision-Language Model
coreMechanism: Connects visual representations with a language model so the system can jointly process images and text.
attention: Visual-language interaction through cross-attention, projection, or joint attention.
feedForward: Vision encoder and language-model feed-forward layers.
routing: Visual representations are projected or routed into the language model.
sequenceModeling: Joint visual and textual token processing.
strengths: Can connect pretrained vision and language components
limitations: Visual token count can be large
Alignment between vision and language representations is challenging

name: Vision-Language Projector
coreMechanism: Maps visual encoder representations into the representation space expected by a language model.
attention: Usually inherited from the vision encoder and language model; the projector itself may be a linear layer or small neural network.
positionEncoding: Inherited from the connected vision and language components.
routing: Visual representations are transformed and inserted into the language-model token stream.
sequenceModeling: Connects visual token sequences with language-token sequences.
strengths: Allows reuse of pretrained vision encoders
Provides a lightweight connection between modalities
limitations: A simple projector may lose fine-grained visual information
Alignment quality depends on multimodal training

name: Prefix Language Model
coreMechanism: Uses bidirectional attention over a prefix while applying causal attention to the generated continuation.
attention: Bidirectional prefix attention combined with causal decoder attention.
routing: Attention mask determines bidirectional and causal regions.
sequenceModeling: Conditional generation from an encoded prefix.
strengths: Combines representation learning and autoregressive generation
limitations: Attention-mask design adds architectural complexity
Less standardized than conventional encoder-only or decoder-only Transformers

name: Denoising Sequence-to-Sequence Architecture
coreMechanism: Corrupts an input sequence and trains an encoder-decoder model to reconstruct the original sequence.
attention: Bidirectional encoder attention, causal decoder attention, and cross-attention.
routing: Encoder representations are routed through decoder cross-attention.
sequenceModeling: Denoising sequence reconstruction.
limitations: More computationally complex than single-stack models
Pretraining corruption strategy influences downstream behavior

name: Retrieval Transformer
coreMechanism: Combines a neural sequence model with an external retrieval mechanism that supplies relevant representations or documents.
attention: Transformer attention over generated tokens and retrieved information.
routing: Retriever determines which external items are provided to the generator.
sequenceModeling: Autoregressive or sequence-to-sequence generation conditioned on retrieved information.
strengths: Extends model knowledge beyond fixed parameters
limitations: Retrieval quality directly affects generation
External indexes introduce infrastructure and latency costs

name: Memory-Augmented Transformer
coreMechanism: Extends Transformer computation with an external or persistent memory mechanism for storing and retrieving representations beyond the immediate context.
attention: Self-attention combined with memory retrieval or memory attention.
routing: Attention or retrieval routes information between active context and memory.
sequenceModeling: Sequence modeling with persistent or extended memory.
strengths: Useful for long documents and sequential environments
limitations: Memory management introduces complexity
Retrieval quality can affect downstream performance

name: Grouped-Query Attention
coreMechanism: Uses fewer key-value heads than query heads so multiple query heads share key-value representations.
attention: Grouped-query attention.
routing: Multiple query groups share key-value states.
sequenceModeling: Standard attention with reduced key-value cache size.
strengths: Improves serving efficiency for autoregressive models
limitations: Can slightly change model quality relative to full multi-head attention
Requires architectural support during training

name: Multi-Query Attention
coreMechanism: Uses a single shared key-value head for multiple query heads.
attention: Multi-query attention.
routing: Multiple query heads share one key-value representation.
sequenceModeling: Attention-based sequence modeling with reduced key-value cache.
limitations: Reduced key-value capacity can affect model quality
Less expressive than fully independent key-value heads

name: Multi-Head Attention
coreMechanism: Computes several attention projections in parallel, allowing different representation subspaces to be modeled simultaneously.
attention: Multiple independent query-key-value attention heads.
positionEncoding: Provided separately by the surrounding architecture.
routing: Each attention head independently routes information between sequence positions.
sequenceModeling: Parallel attention-based interaction between tokens.
strengths: Core mechanism of the original Transformer
limitations: Memory and compute scale with sequence length
Key-value cache can become large during autoregressive inference

name: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation
coreMechanism: Adapts a pretrained model by modifying or adding only a small subset of trainable parameters rather than updating the entire model.
attention: Inherited from the base model.
feedForward: Inherited from the base model, with optional adaptation modules.
routing: Architecture-dependent.
sequenceModeling: Inherited from the pretrained architecture.
strengths: Makes adaptation of large models more practical
limitations: Adaptation capacity can be lower than full fine-tuning
Performance depends on adapter placement and configuration

name: Low-Rank Adaptation
coreMechanism: Injects trainable low-rank matrices into selected model transformations while keeping the original model weights frozen.
attention: Can adapt attention projections of a Transformer.
routing: Inherited from the base model.
sequenceModeling: Inherited from the underlying model.
strengths: Very small number of trainable parameters
Adapters can be stored and exchanged efficiently
limitations: Requires selecting rank and target modules
May not match full fine-tuning for every task

name: Adapter Architecture
coreMechanism: Adds small trainable modules inside a pretrained network while freezing most original parameters.
attention: Inherited from the underlying model.
feedForward: Small trainable adapter modules are inserted into existing transformations.
routing: Information passes through pretrained layers and adapter modules.
sequenceModeling: Inherited from the underlying sequence model.
strengths: Multiple task-specific adapters can share one base model
Reduces storage compared with full model copies
limitations: Adds inference modules
Adapter placement affects performance

name: Quantized Transformer
coreMechanism: Represents model weights or activations using reduced numerical precision to decrease memory and computation requirements.
attention: Inherited from the underlying Transformer.
routing: Inherited from the underlying Transformer.
sequenceModeling: Inherited from the underlying Transformer.
strengths: Can accelerate inference on supported hardware
Enables larger models on constrained hardware
limitations: Aggressive quantization can reduce accuracy
Hardware support varies by precision and implementation

name: Mixture-of-Depths
coreMechanism: Dynamically allocates a limited computation budget so different tokens can traverse different numbers of Transformer layers.
attention: Transformer attention with token-dependent computation allocation.
routing: Learned routing determines which tokens receive additional computation.
sequenceModeling: Adaptive-depth sequence processing.
strengths: Allocates more computation to important tokens
limitations: Routing adds optimization complexity
Uneven computation can complicate efficient hardware execution

name: Speculative Decoding Architecture
coreMechanism: Uses a smaller draft model or auxiliary mechanism to propose multiple tokens that are verified by a larger target model.
attention: Inherited from the target and draft language models.
routing: Draft proposals are routed to the target model for verification.
sequenceModeling: Autoregressive generation with parallel verification of proposed tokens.
strengths: Preserves the target model's output distribution under appropriate verification
Reduces the number of sequential target-model decoding steps
limitations: Speedup depends on draft-model quality
Requires additional model or proposal mechanism
Benefits vary by workload and hardware

name: Agentic Language Model Architecture
coreMechanism: Combines a generative language model with planning, tool invocation, memory, environment interaction, or iterative execution.
attention: Inherited from the underlying language model.
positionEncoding: Inherited from the underlying language model.
feedForward: Inherited from the underlying language model.
normalization: Inherited from the underlying language model.
routing: The model or controller routes actions between reasoning, tools, memory, and environment interaction.
sequenceModeling: Iterative decision and action sequences rather than a single generation pass.
strengths: Can maintain intermediate state or memory
Extends language models into interactive systems
limitations: System behavior depends on tools and orchestration
Long-horizon errors can compound
Agent architecture is broader than the neural model itself

name: Tool-Augmented Language Model
coreMechanism: Allows a language model to invoke external tools or APIs during task execution.
attention: Inherited from the underlying language model.
positionEncoding: Inherited from the underlying language model.
feedForward: Inherited from the underlying language model.
normalization: Inherited from the underlying language model.
routing: Model-generated tool calls route execution to external functions.
sequenceModeling: Alternates between language-model generation and external tool results.
limitations: Tool errors can propagate into the final response
Requires reliable tool interfaces
Tool selection and argument generation can fail

name: Robotic Foundation Model
coreMechanism: Maps multimodal observations and language or task instructions into actions for embodied agents.
attention: Transformer or multimodal attention over visual, language, proprioceptive, and action representations.
positionEncoding: Spatial, temporal, and modality-specific positional representations.
routing: Multimodal representations are routed into action prediction or policy modules.
sequenceModeling: Temporal observation-to-action sequence modeling.
limitations: Real-world interaction data is expensive
Safety and reliability are critical
Sim-to-real transfer can be difficult
